articles.title: As Russian Arms Exports Slide, Central Asia Shops Elsewhere
articles.summary: Central Asian nations are increasingly turning to India, China, Turkey, and Europe for military equipment to reduce their dependence on Russia. Analysts note that this diversification offers greater political flexibility but could create long-term logistical and operational challenges.

articles.title: From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military
articles.summary: Kazakhstan has asked Moscow to help bring home citizens who say they were pressured into signing military contracts to fight in Ukraine. The request puts a fresh spotlight on the vulnerability of Central Asian migrants to Russia’s military enlistment efforts.

articles.title: Kyrgyz Activist Gets 2 Years For Criticizing Growing Chinese Presence
articles.summary: The Lenin District Court in Bishkek found activist and politician Mavlyan Askarbekov guilty and sentenced to two years in prison on offenses related to a law on incitement of racial, ethnic, national, religious, or interregional hatred, a verdict he called "absurd."

articles.title: Kyrgyzstan To Become Spacefaring Nation With Mini Satellite
articles.summary: Kyrgyzstan is set to send a domestically produced satellite into orbit on October 1, marking the Central Asian state's first feat of spacefaring. Uzbekistan has announced its own plans for a domestic satellite.

articles.title: Russia And The Taliban Are Drawing Closer. What's In It For Both Sides?
articles.summary: Russia is deepening diplomatic and military cooperation with Afghanistan's Taliban rulers, driven by security concerns in Central Asia. But worsening Taliban-Pakistan tensions and questions over the scope of Moscow's assistance are complicating the rapprochement.

articles.title: Iran Opens Case Against Satirist Over Khamenei Impression
articles.summary: As the conflict in the Persian Gulf continues to impact and shape the region, journalists from RFE/RL's Central Newsroom and Iranian service, Radio Farda, deliver ongoing updates and analysis.

articles.title: Girls In Hijabs Turned Away From Azerbaijani Schools Amid Protests Over Dress Code
articles.summary: A new dress-code dispute in Azerbaijan’s public schools has sparked protests by parents and students after reports that girls wearing hijabs, or Islamic headscarf, were turned away from classes. The protests come after a new ban on clothing deemed incompatible with the secular nature of education.

articles.title: Ukraine Tests AI-Powered Drones As Debate Grows Over Autonomous Weapons
articles.summary: Ukraine is increasingly using artificial intelligence in drones and other battlefield systems to track, identify, and attack targets. Military officials say humans still remain in control of lethal decisions, but developers warn that fully autonomous weapons are moving closer to reality.

articles.title: Schools In Azerbaijan Turn Away Girls Wearing Hijabs As Debate Over Religious Freedom Intensifies
articles.summary: Azerbaijan’s new school-uniform rules have sparked protests after reports emerged of schools turning away girls wearing hijabs, renewing debate over religious freedom and secular education.

articles.title: EU Working On Multiple Fronts To Limit Russians From Entering Bloc
articles.summary: The European Union is working on multiple fronts to limit the number of Russian citizens that can enter the bloc, including the nuclear option of a total ban on all non-essential travel into the club’s Schengen zone.

articles.title: The Coming Cruel Winter: Ukrainians Brace For The Worst Amid Russia's Escalating Air Campaign
articles.summary: Russia shows no sign of letting up on its escalating aerial campaign against Ukraine’s apartment buildings, bridges, power plants, electricity grid, and other targets. As fall gives way to winter, Kyiv residents are racing to prepare.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Leave At Least 9 Killed As Kyiv Says West Gave No Warning
articles.summary: Deadly Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukraine pounded civilian and energy sites across the country, leaving hundreds of thousands without power despite a cease-fire previously announced by US President Donald Trump.

articles.title: 'We'll Keep Waiting': Afghanistan's Dead-End Road To China
articles.summary: Satellite imagery sourced by RFE/RL confirms Taliban claims they have completed a road that leads up to China's remote border with Afghanistan. However there is no indication Beijing intends to open the militarized boundary any time soon.

articles.title: Russia Pounds Ukraine In Overnight Missile And Drone Attacks
articles.summary: Russia launched overnight missile and drone attacks across Ukraine, striking Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other regions. At least four people were killed in Kharkiv. The attacks came amid a US-proposed energy cease-fire that Moscow has not confirmed.

articles.title: Wider Europe Briefing: What To Expect At The EU's October Summit
articles.summary: In this week's briefing, RFE/RL Europe Editor Rikard Jozwiak drills down on one issue: the upcoming EU summit, with a focus on Ukraine, Russia sanctions, and EU enlargement.

articles.title: Germany Starts Nord Stream 'War Crime' Trial With Prosecutors Blaming Ukrainian 'State Authorities'
articles.summary: After four years of speculation, leaks, and briefings by anonymous sources, the world is finally hearing evidence given publicly under oath in a German courtroom about how the Nord Stream gas pipelines were blown up -- in a case that could prove politically explosive.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Accuses Russia Of Breaking Trump's Cease-Fire On Energy Strikes
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump, in the face of sharp criticism from officials in Ukraine, Europe, and even his Republican party, defended his decision to allow Russian diesel exports and insisted an energy cease-fire between Kyiv and Moscow is in place despite a lack of confirmation from either side.

articles.title: Prominent Iranian Human Rights Lawyer Arrested
articles.summary: A prominent human rights lawyer and activist has been arrested in Iran, sources close to him told RFE/RL’s Radio Farda.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Yandex Strikes Crippled Pro-Kremlin Bots But Tech Experts Question Evidence
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine's recent attacks on Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers have resulted in fewer Internet bots promoting pro-Kremlin hate, a claim that has been disputed by many technology researchers.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Will Stop Refinery Attacks If Russia Halts Energy Strikes
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of striking an energy plant after US leader Donald Trump's surprise announcement of an “energy cease-fire,” while Moscow remained silent on any suggestion of a truce.

articles.title: House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal
articles.summary: Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick plans to force a House vote on legislation blocking Russian oil purchases, challenging President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports as lawmakers warn the move could help finance Moscow's war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Trump Says Ukraine Should 'Get A New President' As Russia Kills At Least 20 In Air Strikes
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for a stalemate in negotiations with Moscow, as Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least 20 people, damaging apartment buildings and energy sites.

articles.title: Is Russia Preparing To Attack The Baltics?
articles.summary: Is Russia about to attack the Baltic states? There are no signs of an imminent conventional invasion, but concerns are growing that Moscow could test NATO in other ways.

By Daud Khattak October 15, 2026 11:27 CET Russia And The Taliban Are Drawing Closer. What's In It For Both Sides? Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Taliban security and defense forces are looking to bolster their arsenal with Russian military hardware. Russian Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev arrived in Islamabad this week for the first official visit by the country’s top domestic affairs official, highlighting growing concerns in Moscow about regional security on its southern flank. Kolokoltsev's visit comes days after a meeting of the Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan -- which also includes Russia, China, India, and Iran -- where Pakistani and Taliban representatives clashed over allegations of their countries’ support for militants who could threaten stability well beyond their borders. Official statements from Islamabad and Moscow have emphasized the strengthening of mutual ties, but analysts said Kolokoltsev’s four-day visit is more about Russia’s fears about the regional presence of Islamic State Khorasan Province (IS-K), known for high-profile assaults including the 2021 Kabul airport bombing, the 2024 Kerman bombings in Iran, and the 2024 Crocus City Hall attack in Russia. Challenging Islamic State While Moscow has been growing diplomatic ties with Kabul in hopes of reining in IS-K, an affiliate of the Islamic State extremist group, Taliban authorities have their eyes fixed on Russian military hardware, including drones, to counterbalance their erstwhile ally, Pakistan. Moscow's increasingly accommodating stance toward the Taliban has sparked widespread international criticism of the group's sweeping restrictions on women's rights and its harsh treatment of political opponents. SEE ALSO: Impoverished Afghans Sell Kidneys On The Black Market 'Out Of Sheer Desperation' “The warming ties between Moscow and Kabul are not part of a new alliance, but a layered regional realignment,” said Omar Samad, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who also served as Afghanistan's ambassador to Canada and France under the previous administration. Russia “gets a low-cost Afghan buffer on Central Asia’s vulnerable flank,” Samad told RFE/RL. “Such cooperation could help Moscow contain threats from Islamic State-Khorasan, Islamic State's regional affiliate and an ideological rival of the Taliban.” Russia's concern about IS-K was highlighted in May by Aleksandr Bortnikov, head of the country’s Federal Security Service (FSB), who warned that the group was recruiting citizens of Central Asian countries and migrant workers inside Russia. In July 2025, Russia became the first country to formally recognize the Taliban government, and it remains the only one to have done so. Unlike in the 1990s, when Russia supplied arms and provided assistance to forces fighting the Taliban, Moscow has come to accept the militant Islamists as a political reality, seeking to protect its security interests in Central Asia, particularly along Afghanistan's northern borders. Cooperation Agreement In May, Russian Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu and Taliban Defense Minister Mohammad Yaqoob signed a military-technical cooperation agreement in Moscow. The agreement's full terms have not been made public, although Yaqoob said it focused on repairing and maintaining Russian-made military equipment already in Afghanistan. In a study published in the Journal of Asian Security and International Affairs in 2025, researchers Tatiana Belousova and Raghav Sharma argued that Moscow's warming relations with the Taliban reflected a pragmatic reassessment of Russia's security interests, particularly its concerns about the threat posed by IS-K. SEE ALSO: Afghan Women Build Businesses As Taliban Restrictions Shrink Their Options But while counterterrorism is a key Russian priority, the Taliban is seeking military assistance to strengthen its defenses, particularly against Pakistani air strikes. After returning from Moscow in late May, Yaqoob said Pakistan would soon no longer dare attack Afghan territory, although he also stressed that the agreement with Russia was not a mutual-defense pact. Pakistan and Taliban forces have repeatedly clashed along their shared border, with tensions escalating after Pakistani air strikes on Kabul and other Afghan locations in October 2025. Pakistan had previously carried out strikes inside Afghanistan, including in March and December 2024. Further strikes and retaliatory attacks followed in 2026. Pakistan, which supported the Afghan Taliban for decades, accuses Kabul of sheltering the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban, an Islamist militant group that has carried out deadly attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians. The Afghan Taliban denies harboring the group. SEE ALSO: Families Torn Apart, Trade At A Standstill: One Year Of The Afghan-Pakistan Border Closure For Moscow, however, counterterrorism remains central to its engagement with Kabul, with recent reports of more direct Russian assistance to Taliban forces. In June, citing two sources within the Taliban's Defense Ministry, Afghanistan International claimed that Russia was helping finance, train, and equip a new 8,000-member Taliban special forces unit. The unit, known as the Hibati Unit, would reportedly conduct operations against IS-K and help secure Afghanistan's border with Pakistan. “Moscow publicly articulates an acute terrorist threat emanating from Afghan soil while simultaneously deepening ties with the Taliban,” geopolitical analyst Eldaniz Gusseinov wrote in The Diplomat. “That is the dual character of the Russian strategy. The threat narrative reinforces a self-assigned security role across Central Asia; the partnership with Kabul provides the instrument for that role.” The Taliban is also said to have stepped up drone surveillance in the northeastern Afghan province of Badakhshan, where armed opposition groups remain active. Russia has not indicated that it is supplying drone technology to the Taliban or assisting in its development. However, Afghanistan International reported on October 1, citing former senior Afghan officials, that the Taliban was seeking to acquire drones and other military equipment from Belarus, a close Russian ally, allegedly with India's financial assistance and Moscow's approval. The claims have not been independently verified. Samad said Russia's growing cooperation with the Taliban had caused unease in Pakistan, although Iran and China shared Moscow's interest in limiting Western military influence in Afghanistan and the wider region. For the Taliban, the benefits are both diplomatic and military, though the latter remains limited in scope. “The Taliban gets formal recognition, support for its counterterrorism and anti-narcotics efforts, and inexpensive help keeping Soviet-era armor and helicopters serviceable, a hedge against Pakistani strikes, not a new arsenal as of yet,” Samad said. (file photo) BRUSSELS -- The European Union is working on multiple fronts to limit the number of Russian citizens that can enter the bloc, including the nuclear option of a total ban on all non-essential travel into the club’s Schengen zone. This comes as Brussels and several EU member states have flagged that individuals using either Russian diplomatic cover or traveling on tourism visas have played key roles in various types of hybrid attacks in the bloc. Most recently, German authorities revealed that the main suspect of the drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, which caused major traffic disruptions, was a Belarusian-Russian citizen who entered the EU using an Italian-issued Schengen tourist visa. In a leaked EU presidency policy paper on various Russian visa options, seen by RFE/RL, it is noted that the “only long-term and effective solution would appear to be the possibility to adopt visa restrictive measures, which would ban non-essential travel for one nationality of applicants.” The document notes that changes to the EU visa code would be necessary for such a move and that “these visa measures would be applied in a uniform way as EU law”. A change to the visa code would be made via qualified majority, constituting 55 percent of all member states, representing 65 percent of the total EU population. A bigger overhaul of the EU visa code could come later in the year but several EU member states, notably in southern Europe, are still reluctant to completely shut down various avenues of people-to-people contact with Russian citizens. SEE ALSO: Wider Europe Briefing: What To Expect At The EU's October Summit Shortly after the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the EU fully suspended the EU-Russia visa facilitation agreement that allowed for cheaper visas, multiple-entry visas and simpler procedures to obtain them. Brussels also issued guidelines to EU member states on how to deal with Russian visa applications, prioritizing so-called “essential travel” requests such as applicants going for humanitarian reasons, including civil society representatives, political dissidents and independent journalists or family reunification. Patchwork Approach These guidelines are nonbinding, giving each EU member state wide discretion on how they would treat Russian visa applications. And the result has created a European patchwork of approaches to Russian visa requests. While many countries on the EU’s eastern flank, bordering Russia, imposed very strict rules by hardly allowing any Russian nationals to enter, southern member states, keen on summer visitors, were more generous in issuing Schengen tourist visas for Russian citizens. In 2025, a record since the full-scale invasion was reached, with 477,878 visas being issued to Russian nationals for tourism purposes. The vast majority of those were authorized by Greece, Italy, France, and Spain. SEE ALSO: Montenegro To Expel Head Of Russian Pro-War Blog Rybar Until a potential decision on a full entry ban could be taken, the EU is working in parallel on three separate tracks on how to reduce the number of Russian visitors -- banning ex-combatants in Ukraine, reducing Russian diplomatic movement and so-called “limited territorial validity (LTV)” visas, which only allows you to stay in the country that issued the visa while prohibiting the holder from travelling to other Schengen zone countries. The presidency paper notes that “LTV visas are presented as an interim measure, pending the future implementation of a full ban on travel for non-essential purposes.” Germany has argued for this approach and the paper notes that the rationale behind the push is to let the countries that still issue non-essential visas to Russian to “assume full responsibility for doing so, in a context where other Member States adopt a much stricter approach.” But the paper also points out the limits with this move, noting that “this runs against one of the basic principles on which the Schengen area is based, i.e. mutual trust. It amounts to a re-nationalization of short-stay visa policy”. Limited Effect The very fact that there hardly are any internal EU border controls also make an LTV visa have limited effect with the document stating that “an LTV visa issued to a Russian national with malevolent intent does not seem to offer sufficient security guarantees against further movements inside the Schengen Area.” Regarding ex-combatants travelling on tourist visas, movement is expected soon. Various European consulates in Russia will most likely be required to check military service documents as part of the visa issuance routine. There are still some issues, however, such as the fact that many of the consulate staff are Russian citizens and that Moscow, according to European diplomats familiar with the matter, has threatened them with legal action if they ask about such documentation. In a separate diplomatic note, seen by RFE/RL, the case for restricting the movement of Russian diplomats and consular staff within the EU is also being explored. The common practice right now stipulates that Russian diplomatic personnel in the EU are only required to notify authorities when traveling to another member state, but there is now a push to introduce a requirement to obtain prior authorization from the country they intend to visit. Another idea gaining traction in Brussels is to limit how long Russian diplomats and officials can remain in their host countries as European counterintelligence services are keen to curb long-established spy networks, in which diplomats stationed in one place for extended periods often play a key role. He previously worked as RFE/RL’s Brussels correspondent, covering numerous international summits, European elections, and international court rulings. He has reported from most European capitals, as well as Central Asia. This item is part of News Russia Europe

https://www.rferl.org/a/azerbaijan-hijab.body: Azerbaijan Schools In Azerbaijan Turn Away Girls Wearing Hijabs As Debate Over Religious Freedom Intensifies By RFE/RL's Azerbaijani Service October 14, 2026 15:50 CET Schools In Azerbaijan Turn Away Girls Wearing Hijabs As Debate Over Religious Freedom Intensifies Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Parents in Baku and elsewhere say school administrations have told girls to remove their head scarves or barred them from classes. (file photo) Parents and students in Azerbaijan are protesting Azerbaijan's new rules on school uniforms following reports that schools were turning away girls wearing hijabs as the dispute over religious freedom and secular education escalated in the Muslim-majority country. The amendment, approved by the Cabinet of Ministers on September 21, prohibits clothing deemed as violating the requirements for school uniforms or conflicting with secular education principles. The hijab is not explicitly mentioned, leaving schools to interpret how the rules apply. Parents in Baku and elsewhere say school administrations have told girls to remove their head scarves or barred them from classes. Some students have boycotted lessons. The Interior Ministry said on October 12 that 37 people had been detained for refusing to comply with the new rules and attempting to disrupt public order. Embed share Girls In Hijabs Turned Away From Azerbaijani Schools Amid Protests Over Dress Code by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:45 0:00 The dispute has escalated an already heated debate in Azerbaijan over whether restricting religious dress in schools protects children from pressure or infringes on their rights. "Children are still in the formation stage. Their worldview, choices, and decisions are often determined by the influence of the family and environment," said Elnara Akimova, a lawmaker from the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), who supported the tightened rules. She told RFE/RL that the amendments were intended to provide a neutral educational environment. But critics argue that the vague application of the rules creates an unnecessary barrier to a child's right to an education. Gulmira Aslanova, a parent in Baku, told RFE/RL that the administration of School No. 172 in the capital's Narimanov district told her to send her daughter to school without a head scarf. She said the restrictions conflicted with constitutional guarantees of religious freedom and education. SEE ALSO: Central Asia's Hijab Debate Flares Up As Schools Reopen "In our country, secondary education is compulsory, and every student must study at school," Aslanova said, adding that those who prevent children from studying should be held accountable. Parents in the southern town of Jalilabad made similar complaints. Sociologist Sanubar Heydarova said children should continue attending school while the legal dispute is resolved. She argued that their right to education should not come at the expense of their cultural identity. Recurring Dispute The controversy echoes a 2010 dispute over school uniforms that did not accommodate the hijab. Hundreds protested in Baku that December, and police broke up subsequent rallies. The controversy continued into 2011. Azerbaijan's constitution defines the country as secular while also safeguarding religious freedom. But the government of the oil-rich nation of some 10.5 million maintains tight control over religious activity. The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), an independent federal commission, recommended in its 2026 annual report that Azerbaijan remain on the State Department's Special Watch List for "severe violations of religious freedom." SEE ALSO: Tajikistan Expands Crackdown On Head Scarves, Beards In New Push For 'National Culture' USCIRF head Vicky Hartzler argued the country should instead be designated a Country of Particular Concern. "Azerbaijan outwardly claims to support religious freedom, yet inwardly does the opposite," Hartzler wrote. She cited government control over religious activity, including the appointment of imams, approval of religious materials, requirements on the registration of churches, and state involvement in writing sermons for Muslim services. Regional Debate Over Religious Dress The dispute has drawn condemnation in Turkey, Azerbaijan's close ally. Protests were held outside Azerbaijan's consulate in Istanbul, while an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said it ⁠was "unacceptable" to deny the right to education for students wearing a hijab. "We expect Azerbaijan to reverse this mistake as soon as possible," the adviser, Oktay Saral, wrote on X. Azerbaijan's ruling party condemned Saral's comments as "irresponsible" and warned they risked ⁠harming relations between the close allies. On social media, some recalled Turkey's own restrictions on head scarves at universities and in public institutions that were gradually lifted between 2010 and 2017. SEE ALSO: Where Did Iran's Hijab Police Go? The hijab has been a point of contention in the region in recent years. In Iran, a historic protest movement Women, Life, Freedom erupted in 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old student, in police custody after being arrested for an allegedly "improper hijab." The movement rapidly transformed from a grievance over state-mandated Islamic dress codes into the most significant challenge to the Islamic republic since the 1979 revolution, fundamentally changing the dynamic between the Iranian public and the ruling regime. Meanwhile in Central Asia, staunchly secular governments have banned or restricted head scarves in schools and workplaces, prompting criticism from Muslim citizens and rights defenders. Officials in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan have been condemned for organizing raids on the streets that targeted women wearing hijabs. https://ashgabat.osce.org/news/centre-as.body: News News Item OSCE lecture course introduces Turkmenistan’s law students to principles of humanitarian law in conflict and post-conflict situations Issued on: 14 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Centre in Ashgabat Fields of work: Human rights , Education Key principles of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in the context of conflict and post-conflict situations were the focus of an OSCE-organized lecture course held in Ashgabat from 12 to 14 October 2026. The three-day course took place at the International University for Humanities and Development (IUHD) and brought together 50 law students and faculty members from the IUHD, the Institute of International Relations (IIR) of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Turkmenistan, and the Institute of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. International experts from Austria shared their expertise in international human rights law, international humanitarian law, international criminal law, and international refugee and migration law, highlighting the distinctive characteristics of these legal frameworks and their relation with national legislation. “The knowledge you have gained during this training course will be useful for your future professional careers and will help you better understand the links between international legal norms, OSCE commitments and their practical application,” said William Leaf, Head of the OSCE Centre in Ashgabat. The lecture course also addressed the protection of women, children and other vulnerable groups; the treatment of detainees and prisoners of war; and the investigation of alleged cases of torture in accordance with international human rights law and international humanitarian law. Students also learned about international accountability mechanisms and approaches to addressing the consequences of human rights violations. https://odihr.osce.org/news/odihr/668703.body: News News Item ODIHR event focuses on supporting Roma rights defenders in Ukraine Issued on: 14 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights Fields of work: Human rights , Roma and Sinti , Tolerance and non-discrimination Roma rights activists discussed how to strengthen their work to combat discrimination and protect human rights during the war in Ukraine at an event organized by the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) in Warsaw. Roma and pro-Roma human rights defenders help combat discrimination and seek remedies for human rights violations affecting Roma. The war following the Russian Federation’s invasion of Ukraine has added to the existing risks, making sustained support for their safety and security essential. “Building and enhancing the capacity of Roma civil society has been a crucial pillar of ODIHR’s intervention in Ukraine. It is of paramount importance to redouble our efforts to provide protection, opportunities and resources for them,” said ODIHR First Deputy Director Tea Jaliashvili. Participants shared their experiences of advocating for the protection and promotion of Roma rights during the war. They discussed how state and non-state stakeholders can better respond to activists’ needs, and how capacity development can support efforts to tackle discrimination and pursue justice. “Legal and policy guarantees alone do not ensure the access of Roma women to healthcare services. A lasting change requires institutional accountability, effective protection against discrimination, and meaningful participation of Roma women in shaping these services intended to meet their needs. The safety of Roma human rights defenders, particularly women, is integral to this work. Documenting violations and advocating for our communities must not subject us to threats, intimidation or reprisals,” said Anna Burdeina, a Roma human rights defender from Ukraine. ODIHR’s support combines training, mentoring and follow-up assistance in human rights monitoring, advocacy, gender empowerment, digital safety and security, and well-being. The three activists speaking at the event are taking part in an ODIHR advocacy programme that has been running since December 2025. The discussion took place at an ODIHR side event during the 2026 Warsaw Human Dimension Conference , as part of the Programme on Support for and Engagement in Ukraine. https://bih.osce.org/news/mission-bosnia.body: News News Item The OSCE Mission and University of Sarajevo join forces to turn human rights education into practice Issued on: 14 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina SARAJEVO, 14 October 2026 – University of Sarajevo students will have the opportunity to learn directly from experts how to address real-life human rights challenges through a new partnership between the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Faculty of Political Sciences. Formalized through a Memorandum of Understanding signed today, the partnership will introduce a semester-long programme for third-year students, scheduled to begin in early 2027. The programme is envisaged to be accredited for 10 ECTS credits and will combine classroom learning with practical experience and insights from professionals working in the field. “Protecting human rights requires more than strong legal frameworks. It also requires professionals who understand how to apply these standards in practice. Through this partnership, we aim to connect academic knowledge with real-life challenges, equip students with practical skills, and contribute to stronger human rights protection in Bosnia and Herzegovina,” said Rick Holtzapple, Head of the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sead Turčalo, Dean of the Faculty of Political Sciences, University of Sarajevo, emphasized that the signing of the Memorandum represents a strategic step in its continued efforts to enhance the quality of education. “Through interactive engagement with experts, work on real-life case studies and mentoring support, our students will acquire practical skills essential for their future professional careers. Our vision at the Faculty of Political Sciences is to educate young people who not only understand contemporary societal challenges but are also equipped with the practical skills needed to address them. This strong partnership with the OSCE Mission enables us to turn that vision into reality.” The partnership will also open opportunities for students from other faculties and disciplines, including Political Science, Sociology, and Journalism and Communications, through expert lectures, workshops, case studies and joint research. The first year of the Memorandum’s implementation will focus on combating violence against women and domestic violence. Through this programme, students will have the opportunity to familiarize themselves with recent legislative developments and gain practical insight into the application of legal provisions and protective measures in this field. By connecting students with practitioners, the initiative aims to prepare future professionals to better recognize, prevent and respond to human rights violations in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

https://montenegro.osce.org/news/mission.body: News News Item OSCE Mission to Montenegro strengthens police capacity for ethical interviewing and evidence recording Issued on: 15 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Montenegro Fields of work: Policing Ethical police interviews and reliable evidence recording are help protect victims’ and witnesses’ rights, ensure fair proceedings, and build public trust in law enforcement. Following request from a broad range of stakeholders, from journalists to the Police Directorate, the OSCE Mission to Montenegro organized a training session in Podgorica on 14 and 15 October on ethical interviewing and the proper use of recording equipment. By the end of the year, the Mission will also provide recording equipment to security departments in Berane, Bijelo Polje, Podgorica and Rožaje. Sixteen police officers took part in the training, guided by a psychologist and a clinical psychologist. They explored techniques for children and adults, the effects of trauma on memory, and ways to safeguard victims’ and witnesses’ rights. Opening the workshop, the Head of the OSCE Mission to Montenegro, Ambassador Jan Haukaas, stated that this training reflected a shared commitment to fair, profession, and lawful police interviews. “The interview is one of the most important tools available to the police. It is often the first point of direct interaction between a person and the police, whether that person is a victim, witness, suspect, journalist or another individual providing information. How this interaction is conducted affects both the reliability of the information obtained and whether the individual feels respected, safe, and able to provide an accurate account” said Ambassador Haukaas. He further stated that “Clear, impartial questioning and careful listening are essential to avoiding misunderstandings, protecting individual rights and ensuring the integrity of investigations.” Assistant Director of Police for the General Jurisdiction Police Sector, Haris Đurđević, noted that the provision and installation of recording equipment was among the requirements under the standards of the Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) that Montenegro is obliged to implement, particularly to protect human rights and vulnerable groups. “This training and the equipment that will be provided by the OSCE Mission represent significant support for the work of the Police Directorate and, at the same time, a safeguard for police officers facing unfounded allegations of abuse and torture,” said Đurđević. The two-day training addressed both the legal and psychological aspects of interviewing, with particular emphasis on engaging with vulnerable groups. It aimed not only to strengthen officers’ practical interviewing skills but also to reinforce their responsibility to uphold professional and legal standards. Properly conducted and recorded interviews contribute to the reliability of evidence, the fairness of criminal proceedings and, ultimately, public trust in the police. The training aimed to strengthen officers’ practical skills and reinforce professional standards, helping to promote reliable evidence, fair proceedings, and greater public confidence in the police. https://odihr.osce.org/news/odihr/668664.body: News News Item New ODIHR handbook brings Roma and Sinti electoral participation into focus at Warsaw conference Issued on: 14 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights Fields of work: Elections , Roma and Sinti , Tolerance and non-discrimination Ensuring that Roma and Sinti can participate meaningfully in elections requires sustained efforts to identify and remove the barriers they continue to face as voters, candidates and participants in public and political life. This was the message from participants at a Warsaw Human Dimension Conference side event organized by the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR). “These challenges remind us that legal guarantees alone are not sufficient. Full and effective participation also requires that we understand how electoral processes operate in practice, identify where barriers exist, and work systematically towards removing them,” said ODIHR First Deputy Director Tea Jaliashvili. The event marked the launch of ODIHR’s new Handbook on Observing and Promoting the Participation of Roma and Sinti in Electoral Processes , developed jointly by ODIHR’s Election Department and Contact Point for Roma and Sinti Issues. Drawing on ODIHR’s longstanding election observation methodology and its work to promote the participation of Roma and Sinti in public and political life, the handbook provides practical guidance on assessing participation throughout the electoral cycle and identifying obstacles that may prevent Roma and Sinti from exercising their electoral rights on an equal basis. Roma and Sinti continue to face a range of barriers to meaningful electoral participation. These can include discrimination and anti-Roma rhetoric, difficulties registering to vote and obtaining identification documents, pressure and vote-buying, limited access to voter information, and under-representation among candidates and elected representatives. Roma and Sinti women and young people may face additional and intersecting barriers to taking part in political and public life. “Meaningful participation is not only about being able to cast a vote. Roma and Sinti need to have a real voice in political life, to stand as candidates, influence decisions and participate on an equal footing. We need to understand the barriers communities experience and ensure that their perspectives are reflected in how electoral processes are designed, assessed and improved,” said Lucie Fuková, Roma activist and former Government Commissioner for Roma Minority Affairs of the Czech Republic. Intended for election observers, public authorities, Roma and Sinti civil society organizations, and other stakeholders, the handbook looks beyond election day to participation throughout the electoral cycle, covering the legal framework, voter and candidate registration, election administration, election campaigns, the media, voting and post-election follow-up. Participants discussed how to put the handbook’s guidance into practice through election observation, civil society monitoring, voter education, advocacy and follow-up to electoral recommendations. They also explored how institutions, civil society and other stakeholders can work together to ensure that the experiences and concerns of Roma and Sinti are systematically reflected in efforts to make electoral processes more inclusive. The first round was on October 4, and the October 25 runoff will feature the current president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and Flávio Bolsonaro. https://cpj.org/2026/10/taliban-suspends.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New York, October 14, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Taliban authorities to immediately and unconditionally restore the FM radio transmissions of British public broadcaster BBC across Afghanistan, end the devastating crackdown on independent media, and cease restricting Afghan’s access to independent news and information. On October 13, the Taliban confirmed that they had suspended BBC World Service programming from FM radio transmitters across Afghanistan, affecting the broadcaster’s Dari, Pashto, and English-language services, according to the BBC and news reports . BBC said it continues to provide news and programming for Afghan audiences in the three languages through shortwave and medium-wave radio, satellite, and online services. “By forcing BBC off Afghanistan’s FM broadcasts, the Taliban are further shrinking an already devastated space for independent journalism in the country,” said Waliullah Rahmani, CPJ’s Afghanistan and Pakistan representative. “The Taliban must immediately reverse the suspension, explain the legal basis for their action, and end their systematic obstruction of Afghans’ access to independent information.” Khabib Ghufran, spokesperson for the Taliban-controlled Ministry of Information and Culture, said the BBC’s activities had been suspended “for the time being” because of what he described as “repeated violations,” without elaborating . London-based broadcaster Afghanistan International reported, citing unnamed sources, that the Taliban’s dissatisfaction with a recent BBC documentary may have contributed to the decision. In March 2022, Taliban authorities ordered local television stations to stop carrying local-language programming from international broadcasters, including the BBC, the U.S. Congress-funded Voice of America, and German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle. The order removed BBC television bulletins in Pashto, Persian, and Uzbek from Afghan partner stations. In December 2022, authorities also removed Voice of America and U.S. Congress-funded Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty from Afghanistan’s AM and FM networks, citing unspecified complaints about their programming. The Taliban Ministry of Information and Culture did not respond to CPJ’s email seeking comment. https://cpj.org/2026/10/cpj-partners-cal.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email The Committee to Protect Journalists joined Albanian and international partner organizations in an open letter calling on Albanian authorities to investigate repeated violence and obstruction affecting journalists covering protests, and ensure accountability. The letter came after serious incidents in the capital Tirana on October 13, when several journalists reported being physically assaulted or obstructed by police officers during protests over education and social issues. Three media workers required hospital treatment. This was not an isolated incident. On October 8, journalists covering a protest outside parliament were obstructed by police despite being identifiable as members of the media, and some were pepper-sprayed. In September , Citizens.al journalist Vjolanda Peca was briefly detained while reporting on a protest. The signatories to the letter called on police, oversight bodies, prosecutors, and government institutions to investigate the incidents, preserve relevant evidence, implement existing journalist safety guidelines, and ensure that journalists can report safely and without obstruction at public assemblies. The letter urged the European Union, Council of Europe, and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) to raise the groups’ concerns with Albanian authorities. It also stressed that effective protection of journalists and implementation of fundamental rights and safeguards are part of Albania’s commitments as part of the process of European Union accession. Read the full open letter here. https://cpj.org/2026/10/turkish-authorit.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Istanbul, October 14, 2026—Turkish authorities must immediately return control of Halk TV, one of the few remaining media voices critical of the government, to its staff and cease their relentless efforts to stifle the free flow of information in the country, the Committee to Protect Journalists said Wednesday. Police officers raided Halk TV’s headquarters in Istanbul Wednesday morning , stopping live broadcasts and preventing staff from entering the building, although some posted on X that they were later allowed in. Halk TV said on X that authorities assigned a trustee, or administrator, to take over the outlet, while news reports said the raid was linked to a criminal investigation into owner Cafer Mahiroğlu , whose other assets were seized as well. Mahiroğlu, who lives abroad, said in a video message on X that seven of his relatives in Turkey were in police custody, and that the accusations against him were false. “Seizing Halk TV strikes at the heart of press freedom in Turkey where the vast majority of news outlets are pro-government. Halk TV is one of the very few remaining broadcasters that criticize the government and this action is a devastating blow to the Turkish people’s right to freedom of information and expression,” said Özgür Öğret, CPJ’s Turkey representative. “Control of Halk TV must immediately be returned to its staff and this deeply alarming and damaging crackdown on journalism must end.” Turkey is witnessing an intense and sustained crackdown on independent and pro-opposition media, with dozens of journalists arrested or detained so far this year. Turkish authorities have also blocked access to thousands of social media accounts belonging to journalists and rights defenders. In October last year, authorities also seized the TELE1 broadcaster and appointed a trustee. At the time of publication, Halk TV’s website and its social media accounts were still being run by staff while the TV station was broadcasting music and documentaries. But a court ordered all Halk TV’s social media accounts to be blocked to access from Turkey, local media reported. In a statement, the Chief Prosecutor’s Office in Istanbul said Mahiroğlu was under investigation for “bribery, collusion tendering, and laundering criminally obtained assets.” The statement said an arrest warrant had been issued for Mahiroğlu and 16 other suspects. According to the statement, companies that Mahiroğlu is a partner of or a director at, alongside companies that he has ties to, were all seized by a court order. CPJ emailed the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office for comment but did not receive a reply. https://rsf.org/fr/comment-le-kremlin-im.body: Comment le Kremlin impose son récit de la guerre à la génération Z chinoise : plongée dans la couverture de l’Ukraine sur Bilibili RSF Comment le Kremlin impose son récit de la guerre à la génération Z chinoise : plongée dans la couverture de l’Ukraine sur Bilibili Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel À l’origine, Bilibili, l’équivalent chinois de YouTube, était une plateforme destinée aux amateurs de dessins animés japonais. Aujourd’hui, elle est devenue l’un des principaux sites de vidéos en ligne qui façonnent la vision du monde de la génération Z chinoise. Les discours favorables au Kremlin y bénéficient d’une audience étonnamment importante. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) a constaté que leur diffusion était alimentée par des blogueurs chinois très populaires, sur une plateforme qui ne modère guère les contenus faux et préjudiciables, ainsi que par les médias de propagande russes, qui figurent parmi les très rares médias étrangers à y être présents. « La défaite de la Russie n’est, pour l’instant, qu’un fantasme de l’Union européenne (UE) et de l’Ukraine. » Pour Lú Kèwén, blogueur chinois populaire qui couvre régulièrement la guerre en Ukraine auprès des 4,6 millions d’abonnés de sa chaîne sur Bilibili, cela ne fait aucun doute. Alors que l’Ukraine s’enfonce dans un « bourbier de dettes », la Russie a « encore des cartes à jouer », qui lui permettent de repousser les « négociations de paix ». Publiée en juin 2026, cette vidéo de Lú Kèwén, qui reprend le discours du Kremlin, avait enregistré près d’un demi-million de vues deux mois plus tard, en août 2026. Lancée en 2009, la plateforme chinoise de partage de vidéos Bilibili regorge de contenus consacrés à l’invasion à grande échelle de l’Ukraine par la Russie. Et leur orientation est clairement favorable à Moscou. RSF a constaté que, près de cinq ans après le début de cette invasion, Bilibili hébergeait aussi bien des vidéos montrant des scènes de violence particulièrement crues sur le front que des images du dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong-un accueillant des soldats de retour du front, où ils avaient combattu aux côtés des forces russes. Cet espace numérique est investi par des blogueurs chinois comme Lú Kèwén, qui commente la guerre en présentant Vladimir Poutine comme un « dirigeant fort » et Volodymyr Zelensky comme une « marionnette de l’Occident », mais aussi par les médias d’État russes. D’un site consacré aux mangas à une plateforme grand public qui informe la génération Z Bilibili a été lancé en 2009 comme un site destiné aux amateurs de dessins animés japonais. En 2018, l’entreprise a fait son entrée au Nasdaq, la Bourse américaine. Cette étape a marqué le début de sa transformation : d’une plateforme de niche centrée sur la communauté des amateurs d’animation, de bandes dessinées et de jeux vidéo (ACG), Bilibili est devenue un site proposant une grande diversité de contenus vidéo, notamment dans les domaines de la technologie, du mode de vie et de la mode. Bilibili revendiquait environ 366 millions d’utilisateurs actifs mensuels en 2025, qui passaient en moyenne 107 minutes par jour sur l’application. La plateforme cible activement les jeunes de la génération Z, généralement définie comme celle des personnes nées après 1997. Selon l’entreprise, 70 % des membres de cette génération en Chine regardaient Bilibili en 2024. Son chiffre d’affaires annuel net avoisine 4,34 milliards de dollars. À titre de comparaison, les revenus de YouTube ont dépassé 60 milliards de dollars en 2025. L’audience de Bilibili se trouve principalement en Chine. Au fil des années, cette plateforme initialement dédiée au divertissement est devenue un vecteur majeur de diffusion de récits géopolitiques auprès du jeune public sinophone. Des politiques de Donald Trump aux éloges adressés à Evgueni Prigojine, homme d’affaires russe proche de Vladimir Poutine avant sa mort en 2023, les vidéos consacrées à la politique internationale cumulent les vues et fidélisent un large public. Un écosystème chinois aligné sur le Kremlin En analysant plus d’une centaine de vidéos publiées sur Bilibili et consacrées à la guerre en Ukraine, aux politiques de Vladimir Poutine et de Volodymyr Zelensky ainsi qu’aux deux armées, RSF a constaté que la grande majorité d’entre elles reprenaient des éléments de langage favorables au Kremlin. On y trouve notamment des moqueries visant Volodymyr Zelensky et la mobilisation en Ukraine, des justifications de l’invasion ou d’exécutions commises sur le front, ainsi que des manifestations d’admiration pour la « force politique » de Vladimir Poutine. Le blogueur Lú Kèwén est également l’auteur de la vidéo la plus populaire de la plateforme consacrée à l’invasion à grande échelle de l’Ukraine par la Russie. Intitulée « Quel grand jeu de puissances se cache derrière l’étrange conflit russo-ukrainien ? », elle a été publiée le 24 février 2022, jour même du déclenchement de l’invasion russe. À l’été 2026, elle totalisait plus de 11 millions de vues. Le discours est sans ambiguïté. « Du point de vue russe, cette région stratégique [l’Ukraine] nous appartenait à l’origine, la plupart de ses habitants sont russes, alors je ne fais que la reprendre. Et alors ? », affirme le blogueur, reprenant l’argumentaire de Vladimir Poutine pour justifier l’invasion. Il dépeint une Russie puissante, dirigée d’une « main de fer » par Vladimir Poutine, face à une Ukraine réduite au rôle de « marionnette ». Cette mise en scène est récurrente dans ses vidéos comme dans leurs vignettes de présentation : Vladimir Poutine y apparaît, par exemple, souriant, tandis que le président ukrainien Volodymyr Zelensky est représenté l’air triste et impuissant. Screenshots of Bilibili video thumbnails promoting pro-Russian narratives. © [Bilibili/Lú Kèwén, War Research Institute ], screenshots taken by RSF, August 2026. D’autres blogueurs chinois ont adopté un style similaire pour illustrer leurs vidéos, parfois en recourant à l’intelligence artificielle. Un blogueur chinois comptant 563 000 abonnés, qui se fait appeler « War Research Institute » (« Institut de recherche sur la guerre »), a ainsi généré une image de Volodymyr Zelensky en pleurs à l’aide de l’IA pour illustrer une vidéo consacrée aux désertions dans l’armée ukrainienne. Ces dernières années, la mobilisation en Ukraine est en effet devenue l’un des thèmes de prédilection de la propagande russe. Le groupe Wagner, organisation de mercenaires russes fondée par Evgueni Prigojine, qui constituait au début de l’invasion à grande échelle l’un des piliers de la propagande russe, figure parmi les sujets favoris des blogueurs chinois couvrant la guerre sur la plateforme. Une vidéo montrant Evgueni Prigojine s’emporter contre le commandement militaire russe en raison d’une pénurie de munitions a ainsi recueilli près de 2,5 millions de vues. Certains utilisateurs se filment en train de reproduire en russe sa tirade furieuse, tandis que d’autres le transforment en véritable mème, le réinventant sous les traits d’un personnage de dessin animé japonais dansant sur de la musique. Une manière de faire de lui une figure de la culture populaire, alors même que le groupe Wagner a commis des crimes de guerre en Ukraine et dans d’autres pays, notamment en Syrie et en République centrafricaine. Plusieurs blogueurs chinois ont également décrit Evgueni Prigojine comme une « figure marquante de sa génération ». Screenshots of Bilibili video thumbnails depicting Yevgeny Prigozhin. © [Bilibili/A Tun Ah, TV90_InOffishul ], screenshots taken by RSF, August 2026. Des médias pro-Kremlin présents sur la plateforme Les blogueurs chinois ne sont pas les seuls à diffuser des discours favorables au Kremlin. Sur Bilibili, la présence officielle de médias d’État étrangers se limite, dans les faits, presque exclusivement aux médias russes pro-Kremlin RT et Sputnik. https://rsf.org/fr/ukraine-des-for%C3%AA.body: Ukraine : des forêts brulées aux sols minés, le journalisme environnemental bouleversé par la guerre russe Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Forêts minées ou occupées, incendies massifs, écosystèmes détruits... En Ukraine, depuis l'invasion russe à grande échelle en 2022, les sujets traités par les journalistes environnementaux ont radicalement changé. De Lviv à Mykolaïv, en passant par Kyiv, des professionnels des médias documentent désormais les conséquences environnementales de la guerre, contournant l’accès au terrain limité avec les combats. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) s’est entretenue avec plusieurs d’entre eux. Lire en ukrainien / Читати українською “Avant l’invasion russe à grande échelle, j’écrivais sur les conséquences environnementales de l’introduction de la culture de riz en Ukraine” , se souvient la journaliste Mariana Verbovska , spécialisée depuis plus de 20 ans dans les questions environnementales. Mais depuis février 2022, ses sujets portent les stigmates de la guerre, entre la mer Noire polluée et les forêts détruites. Au début de l’invasion, elle s’était d’abord interrogée : “Est-ce que les gens se préoccupent de l’environnement en temps de guerre ?” Son hésitation fut de courte durée. En 2023, alors qu’elle était plongée dans le noir à Lviv, dans l’ouest du pays, avec les frappes massives russes contre les infrastructures énergétiques ukrainiennes, un reporter en Allemagne lui demande d’écrire sur la mort des dauphins en mer Noire en raison de la guerre. Au départ, le sujet lui paraît “déplacé” par rapport à ce qu’endure la population. Puis, elle réalise que si elle ne l’écrit pas, personne ne le fera. Elle enquête donc pour le média d’investigation local de Lviv, NGL.media . “Alors que des pans entiers du territoire ukrainien sont devenus inaccessibles avec les combats et l’occupation russe, les journalistes environnementaux couvrent les conséquences écologiques de la guerre. Leur travail est essentiel : il informe le public aujourd’hui et contribue à établir l’ampleur des destructions. Pour poursuivre leur mission d’intérêt général, ces médias doivent être soutenus financièrement. Pauline Maufrais Chargée de zone Ukraine chez RSF Enquêter depuis le ciel Fin 2025, les conséquences environnementales causées par la guerre russe en Ukraine auraient atteint les 43 milliards de dollars (environ 38 milliards d’euros), selon une étude ukrainienne réalisée par un collectif indépendant d’experts, l’Initiative pour la comptabilisation des émissions de gaz à effet de serre liées à la guerre, préparée avec le soutien de l’organisation environnementale ukrainienne Ekodia. L’une des coordinatrices de l’organisation non gouvernementale, Anna Koriahina, estime que “la place accordée aux effets environnementaux de la guerre a considérablement augmenté dans les médias” , même si ces sujets restent dans l’ensemble “sous traités” par les rédactions. L’une des raisons est que l’accès à l’information est “difficile” , rappelle Anna Koriahina. Près de 20 % du pays est de fait occupé par la Russie . Le long de la ligne de front est inaccessible en raison des combats, des mines et du risque des drones, et les territoires occupés sont fermés aux journalistes indépendants, qui sont systématiquement arrêtés par Moscou . À cela, s’ajoutent parfois les restrictions d’information des autorités ukrainiennes “pour des impératifs de sécurité” . Face à ces obstacles, des reporters enquêtent depuis le ciel. Les images satellites sont devenues un outil central. Mariana Verbovska a par exemple eu recours aux images satellitaires du programme européen Copernicus lorsqu’elle a voulu vérifier une affirmation du ministère ukrainien chargé de l’Environnement selon laquelle 30 % des forêts du pays étaient occupées ou détruites. Impossible d’aller mesurer les dégâts sur place : “Il y a énormément de mines, peu de gens peuvent y accéder”. Elle écrit alors aux entreprises états-uniennes spécialisées dans l’imagerie satellite Maxar et Planet Labs. Avec un datajournaliste, elle obtient l’accès à leurs données pour enquêter. Résultat, le chiffre de 30 % est surestimé. “C’est justement notre travail de vérifier ces affirmations”, rappelle la reporter . Documenter les crimes environnementaux À Kyiv, la journaliste environnementale Viktoriia Hubareva , qui travaille pour le média de solution Rubryka , utilise aussi les images du programme européen Copernicus pour documenter les destructions d’écosystèmes, en particulier estimer les surfaces brûlées. “Nos publications peuvent servir à l’avenir de preuves des crimes russes contre l’environnement, dans un objectif de réparations économiques de la Russie” , explique-t-elle. Son travail peut notamment alimenter des enquêtes judiciaires ouvertes pour “écocide”, notion qui a été inscrite dans la législation ukrainienne dès 2001, mais encore peu appliquée. Leur travail permet de garder la mémoire des lieux inaccessibles. “Les personnes qui ont connu ces endroits se demandent ce qu’elles vont voir quand elles pourront revenir” , raconte Viktoriia Hubareva. Avec des scientifiques, elle a par exemple documenté les incendies sur la presqu’île de Dzharlylhach, au sud-est de Kherson. “Nous avons été les premiers à les documenter. Personne n’était encore au courant.” Les sujets se multiplient dans le pays. À Mykolaïv, ville du sud-est, à environ 70 kilomètres du front, une journaliste qui travaille pour le média local NikVesti, Yuliia Boichenko , a commencé à couvrir les sujets environnementaux au moment de l'invasion à grande échelle. Là-bas, les conséquences environnementales de la guerre se sont manifestées en touchant une ressource essentielle : l’eau . Après une frappe russe en 2022 sur la conduite alimentant la ville depuis le fleuve Dnipro, Mykolaïv et ses quelque 500 000 habitants sont privés d’approvisionnement. Le recours à l’eau d’une autre rivière de la région pouvant présenter des risques sanitaires est devenu pour elle un sujet au long cours. Une empreinte bien au-delà de la guerre Ces articles intéressent les lecteurs parce que “l’environnement affecte leur avenir”. “C’est nous qui allons devoir y vivre” , souligne Yuliia Boichenko. “Malgré la menace existentielle qui pèse sur nous, nous vivons dans un pays où les gens veulent améliorer leur environnement immédiat” , ajoute Viktoriia Hubareva. Or, de nombreux effets de la guerre sur l’environnement restent à mesurer. Mariana Verbovska cite notamment les kilomètres de fibre optique déroulés sur les régions proches du front par les drones russes comme ukrainiens qui s’accumulent sur les sols. “Il ne s’agit pas de dire si nous devons les utiliser ou non, nous sommes contraints par un cadre militaire” , précise-t-elle. Leur coût environnemental reste inconnu bien que les sols ukrainiens subissent déjà les traces de leur passage. https://www.hronikatm.com/2026/10/privat.body: ХТ Частные строительные компании не могут погасить кредиты, а сотни семей — получить жилье Редакция 14 октября 2026 1571 Важное Лента Редакция - 15 октября 2026 Президент Туркменистана прибыл с визитом в Азербайджан Лента Редакция - 15 октября 2026 Аркадаг проиграл Аль-Джазире Лента Редакция - 13 октября 2026 Россельхознадзор Омской области уничтожил 18 тонн зараженных томатов из Туркменистана ХТ Редакция - 13 октября 2026 Напасти в городе Туркменбаши Рядом с городом Аннау (Änew) и селом Гями (Gämi), расположенными недалеко от Ашхабада, построены четыре многоквартирных дома по государственному заказу. В каждом из них — по 48 квартир. Однако уже несколько месяцев около 200 семей не могут заселиться в новое жилье. Проблемы возникли и у строительных компаний, которые не могут вернуть банковские кредиты. Как сообщают корреспонденты «Хроники Туркменистана», представители государственных органов, ответственные за подписание актов приемки завершенных объектов, до сих пор не сделали этого. Причины задержки они не объясняют ни строителям, ни будущим жильцам. Обычно частные строительные компании берут банковские кредиты для выполнения работ. После завершения строительства заказчик оплачивает выполненный проект, а подрядчики погашают задолженность перед банками. В нынешней ситуации компании не могут получить оплату за построенные дома и своевременно рассчитаться с кредиторами. В результате на задолженность начисляются пени за просрочку платежей, а строительные фирмы теряют прибыль. Подобные случаи на строительном рынке происходят все чаще. Ранее сообщалось , что в городе Аркадаг акты приемки завершенных зданий не выдавали более года. В результате представители строительного бизнеса сталкиваются с финансовыми трудностями. Некоторые из них закрывают компании и покидают страну. https://rsf.org/fr/à-l-approche-des-500-.body: À l’approche des 500 jours, la mobilisation s’accélère pour que Christophe Gleizes retrouve enfin les siens Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel À l’approche des 500 jours de détention de Christophe Gleizes en Algérie, sa famille, son comité de soutien et Reporters sans frontières (RSF) réaffirment leur détermination à obtenir sa libération et annoncent de prochaines mobilisations publiques. Face à une situation qui demeure sans issue à ce jour, ils renouvellent leur appel au président algérien Abdelmadjid Tebboune à faire preuve de clémence et enfin accorder sa grâce au journaliste sportif français, collaborateur des médias So Foot et Society. Ce jeudi 15 octobre, au siège de Reporters sans frontières (RSF), la famille de Christophe Gleizes a pris la parole lors d’une conférence de presse pour appeler de nouveau à la fin de l’enfermement du professionnel de l’information. Elle s’exprimait pour la première fois depuis l’été, à son retour d’Algérie, où elle avait pu rendre visite, le 4 octobre dernier, au journaliste détenu à la prison de Koléa. Incarcéré depuis le 29 juin 2025, Christophe Gleizes, collaborateur des magazines français So Foot et Society , a été condamné à sept ans de prison pour avoir exercé son métier de journaliste. “On ne comprend pas ce qu’il se passe. Quand nous nous manifestons publiquement, cela suscite la colère. Quand nous gardons le silence, il ne se passe rien, quand nous faisons appel à la mansuétude du président Tebboune, aucune réponse. Pendant ce temps, l’horloge tourne, un journaliste reste emprisonné et la santé de sa grand-mère de 102 ans qui l’attend se dégrade. Franchement, c’est insupportable. Une chose est certaine : nous sommes plus que jamais résolus à obtenir la libération de notre fils, Christophe. Sylvie et Francis Godard Parents de Christophe Gleizes La visite des parents de Christophe Gleizes à leur fils, en septembre dernier, était leur septième depuis son incarcération. Début juillet, puis en août, le frère et la compagne de Christophe ont aussi pu lui rendre visite. Christophe Gleizes reçoit également des visites du consul de France et du cardinal Vesco. “Nous sommes ses seuls liens avec le monde extérieur” , souligne sa famille qui avec RSF et le comité de soutien invite toutes celles et ceux qui souhaitent manifester leur solidarité à écrire directement à Christophe en prison (Christophe Gleizes, Numéro d’écrou : 54118, Établissement pénitentiaire de Koléa, Tipaza 42 000, Algérie) “Quand on a informé Christophe des mobilisations pour sa libération, il nous a dit à quel point il se sent redevable, et veut être à la hauteur de tout cet élan de solidarité. Votre mobilisation compte pour lui, elle l’aide à tenir, cela lui donne de la force.” soulignent ses parents. “Christophe serait-il otage d’État ? Comment expliquer que le président algérien n’ait pas prononcé une grâce alors que le dossier est vide et que la voie judiciaire est épuisée ? La situation de Christophe est un drame humain, avant tout, et elle est épouvantable. Je tiens à saluer la pudeur et la dignité de sa famille, mais elle cache une immense douleur. Christophe doit être rendu à sa famille et à son travail. Après la finale de la Coupe de France dédiée à Christophe, le soutien déterminant du président de la FFF Philippe Diallo puis du président de la FIFA Gianni Infantino et les mots du sélectionneur de l’équipe de France Zinédine Zidane, RSF en a sous la pédale et accélère sa campagne publique, avec de nouvelles mobilisations de premier plan prévues à l’approche des 500 jours d’emprisonnement le 11 novembre. Thibaut Bruttin Directeur général de RSF Appel aux collectivités et aux soutiens Après Agen, ville de naissance de Christophe Gleizes, la Ville de Paris, où il vit et travaille, a à son tour témoigné de son soutien au journaliste en votant, le 8 octobre, à l’unanimité pour que Christophe devienne “citoyen d’honneur” de la capitale française. Sa famille et son comité de soutien saluent cet engagement transpartisan exemplaire et appellent désormais l'ensemble des collectivités territoriales françaises à rejoindre le mouvement pour sa libération. Elles sont aussi appelées à s’engager avec leurs homologues algériennes dans le cadre de leur coopération décentralisée ou de leurs jumelages, pour appeler à la libération du journaliste Christophe Gleizes. Un match de foot en soutien à Christophe Pour marquer les 500 jours de détention, RSF et le comité de soutien organisent un match solidaire le 11 novembre prochain. Vingt-deux footballeurs et footballeuses professionnels ou amateurs, des journalistes, des figures du monde de la culture et des personnalités publiques se retrouveront autour d’un match symbolique, placé sous le signe de la convivialité et de l’engagement, pour rappeler une évidence : la place de Christophe Gleizes, journaliste sportif, est sur les terrains et dans les tribunes de presse, pas en prison. Chronologie de l’affaire Christophe Gleizes et de la mobilisation pour sa libération : 28 mai 2024 : arrestation de Christophe Gleizes à Tizi Ouzou (Algérie) alors qu’il faisait un reportage sur le club JS Kabylie (JSK). Il est placé sous contrôle judiciaire. 29 juin 2025 : condamnation du journaliste français spécialiste de football Christophe Gleizes à sept années de prison ferme avec mandat de dépôt pour “apologie du terrorisme” et “possession de publications dans un but de propagande nuisant à l'intérêt national”. 30 juin 2025 : lancement d’une pétition par RSF pour appeler à la libération de Christophe Gleizes. Elle recueille, à ce jour, plus de 34 000 signatures. 16 juillet 2025 : une centaine de personnalités publiques soutiennent l’appel à la libération du journaliste Christophe Gleizes, injustement condamné à sept ans de prison en Algérie. 24 juillet 2025 : lors du passage du Tour de France, une banderole géante appelant à la libération de Christophe Gleizes est déployée – action coordonnée par RSF. L’objectif : transformer l’un des événements sportifs les plus médiatisés de l’année en tribune pour la liberté de la presse. Août 2025 : une bâche géante en soutien au journaliste Christophe Gleizes déployée sur le fronton de la mairie d’Agen, sa ville de naissance. L’appel à la libération de Christophe a aussi été partagé lors des festivals d’Avignon, Rock en Seine, Couthures-sur-Garonne... avec des interventions des membres du comité de soutien et RSF. 29 septembre 2025 : pour appeler, à l’occasion du troisième mois de détention du journaliste sportif Christophe Gleizes en Algérie, à sa libération, 16 écoles de journalisme françaises se mobilisent conjointement. RSF salue cette initiative et renouvelle également son appel à la libération du professionnel de l’information, spécialiste de football. 20 novembre 2025 : neuf clubs de football de Ligue 1 mobilisés pour la libération de Christophe Gleizes détenu en Algérie. 29 novembre 2025 : près de 30 personnalités unissent leurs voix pour appeler à la libération du journaliste français enfermé en Algérie. 3 décembre 2025 : procès en appel de Christophe Gleizes à la cour d’appel de Tizi Ouzou, qui a confirmé la peine de sept ans de prison ferme . RSF renouvelle son appel pour sa libération. 18 décembre 2025 : dévoilement d’un visuel géant à l’effigie de Christophe sur la façade du siège de la Fédération française de football (FFF) à Paris. Les 19, 20 et 21 décembre, lors des 32e de finale de la Coupe de France, des messages de soutien sont diffusés, dont un message vidéo de la mère de Christophe Gleizes, Sylvie Godard, adressé à son fils, à la 7e minute du match Paris Saint-Germain – Fontenay-le-Comte, un temps fort symbolique 29 janvier 2026 : une soirée exceptionnelle de soutien a été organisée au Bataclan, afin de marquer les sept mois de détention de Christophe Gleizes. Réunissant plus de 1 000 spectateurs et animée par la journaliste Ambre Godillon, cette soirée a réuni sur scène des artistes engagés qui ont choisi de se produire à titre grac

Бұл жөнінде зерттеушілерге сүйенген Reuters агенттігі жазды . Ақпарат агенттігі бұл оқиғаны "кішірек көрші елдің Мәскеуге қарсы жасаған кибертыңшылығына сирек мысал" деп сипаттайды. Reuters-тің жазуынша, Cisco компаниясының зерттеушісі Чи-энь Шен мен Recorded Future киберқауіпсіздік компаниясының маманы Джулиан-Фердинанд Фогеле бірлесіп әзірлеген есепте Silent Lynx ("Ізсіз сілеусін") хакерлік тобының "Қазақстанда орналасуы ықтимал" екені жазылған. Бұған дейін бұл топ Орталық Азия елдеріндегі мемлекеттік ұйымдардың жүйелерін де бұзған. Зерттеушілердің мәліметінше, Silent Lynx көбіне "мақсатты фишинг" (spear phishing) әдісін қолданады. Хакерлер маңызды құжаттарға ұқсайтын тіркемелері бар электронды хаттар жібереді. Пайдаланушы сол файлдарды абайсызда ашқан жағдайда, оның құрылғысына зиянды бағдарлама жүктеледі. Джонс Хопкинс университетінің Халықаралық зерттеулер жөніндегі жоғары мектебінің докторанты Олег Шакировтың пікірінше, бұл кибертыңшылықпен тек жетекші кибердержавалар ғана айналыспайтынын көрсетеді. "Басқа елдер де өз мүмкіндіктерін біртіндеп арттырып келеді" деді ол Reuters-ке. Зерттеушілердің хабарлауынша, Silent Lynx тобы Ресейдің оңтүстігіндегі "Орскнефтеоргсинтез" мұнай өңдеу зауытына кибершабуыл жасаған. Бұл кәсіпорын тамызда украин дронының соққысынан кейін бірнеше айға жұмысын тоқтатқан еді. Бұған қоса, зерттеушілердің мәліметінше, хакерлер Мәскеуден шығысқа қарай шамамен 425 шақырым жерде орналасқан Нижний Новгород қаласы әкімшілігінің ақпараттық жүйелеріне де қол жеткізген. "Орскнефтеоргсинтез" мұнай өңдеу зауыты Қазақстан шекарасынан шамамен 25 шақырым жерде орналасқан. Украин дрондарының шабуылы салдарынан өндіріс бірнеше рет тоқтағандықтан Ресей билігі Қазақстаннан мұнай өңдеу нысандарын пайдалануды сұраған еді. Ор қаласындағы мұнай өңдеу зауытының өкілдері және Нижегород облысының әкімшілігі Reuters-ке түсініктеме бермеді. Хакерлермен байланысу да мүмкін болмады. Зерттеушілер Silent Lynx тобының Қазақстанға қатысы бар деген болжамды бірнеше дерекпен дәлелдеуге тырысады. Атап айтқанда, хакерлер зиянды бағдарламаның кодын құрастырғаннан кейін көп ұзамай оны Қазақстан аумағынан сынап көруге әрекеттенген. Бұған қоса, топтың белсенділігі Қазақстандағы жұмыс уақытымен да сәйкес келеді. Бұдан бөлек, сарапшылар хакерлердің әрекеттері Қазақстанның стратегиялық мүдделерімен үндесетінін де атап өтеді. Reuters келтірген зерттеушілердің мысалына қарағанда, 2026 жылдың басында Қазақстан Тәжікстанмен жасалған келісімді ратификациялаған шақта хакерлер осы елдің мемлекеттік органының ақпараттық жүйесін бұзған. Осыған ұқсас жағдай Беларусьте де болды: Беларусьтегі мемлекеттік органның ақпараттық жүйесі сәуірде – Беларусь пен Қазақстан дипломаттарының кездесуі қарсаңында бұзылды. Қазақстан, Ресей, Тәжістан, Беларусь үкіметтері ақпарат агенттігінің сұрақтарына жауап бермеді.
